items.bodyEn: Hamamatsu, the twenty-ninth post town, was the castle town where Tokugawa Ieyasu lived for seventeen years, from 1570 to 1586, before he ruled Japan. So many later lords of the castle rose to high office that it was nicknamed Shusse-jō, 'castle of promotions'. Hiroshige drew the station in winter: travelers warming at a bonfire under a towering pine.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō No. 30 Hamamatsu: Fuyugare no zu; 東海道宿村大概帳

items.bodyEn: This station is famous for wind. Enshū no karakkaze, the dry wind of Enshū, the region's old name, blows hard from the northwest across the Hamamatsu plain from late autumn to early spring, after the mountains have wrung out its moisture. Kara means empty or dry; the wind parches the fields and gives the winter sky its clear blue.

雷 (kaminari), thunder, is a native compound: kami, god, plus nari, the stem of naru, to sound or rumble. Thunder was the gods making noise, and the Chinese character 雷 was simply fitted onto that word. Its partner 稲妻 (inazuma), lightning, is 'the rice plant's spouse', from the old belief that lightning made the ears of rice ripen.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (日本国語大辞典), entries 雷 (かみなり) and 稲妻

items.bodyEn: In 神 the left side, 示, is an altar; the right side, 申, was originally a drawing of a lightning bolt zigzagging through the sky. Divinity, then, is lightning at the altar. The same bolt sits under 雨, rain, in 電, the kanji for electricity, which still means lightning in words such as 電光, a lightning flash.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entries 神 and 申; 新字源 on the oracle-bone form of 申
